title: Bayes' Theorem Basics
tagline: Year 3 — Updating a probability after evidence: total probability, tree diagrams and reverse conditioning

introduction.overview: Bayes' theorem reverses a conditional probability. If you know how likely an outcome is under each of several causes, it tells you how likely each cause is once the outcome is seen. It uses the law of total probability for the denominator: the overall chance of the outcome across all causes. A tree diagram or a table of counts makes the calculation straightforward.
introduction.placementRelevance: Bayes-type questions are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds as "a bag is chosen at random and a ball is drawn… find the probability that it came from bag 1".
introduction.realWorldContext: Diagnosing a disease from a test result, spam filters and fault tracing in manufacturing use the same reasoning.

learningObjectives: Compute the total probability of an event across several causes
Apply Bayes' formula to find the probability of a cause
Use a tree diagram or count table to organise the work
Avoid confusing P(A | B) with P(B | A)

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: P(A and B) = P(A) P(B | A) = P(B) P(A | B). Causes are mutually exclusive and cover all possibilities.

coreDefinitions: Prior probability: the probability of a cause before the evidence.
Total probability: P(E) = Σ P(Hᵢ) P(E | Hᵢ).
Bayes' theorem: P(Hⱼ | E) = P(Hⱼ) P(E | Hⱼ) / Σ P(Hᵢ) P(E | Hᵢ).
Posterior probability: the probability of a cause after the evidence.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Imagine 1000 trials. Split them among the causes by their priors, then see how many of each cause produce the evidence. Bayes' answer is simply the share of the evidence cases that came from the cause you ask about.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Make a count table: take a convenient total, split by priors, apply the likelihoods, and divide the cause's count by the total evidence count.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Tree diagram
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Multiply along branches, add across branches

mainNarrative: First find the total probability of the evidence. Bag 1 has 3 red and 2 blue balls; bag 2 has 2 red and 3 blue. A bag is chosen at random and a ball drawn. P(red) = ½ × 3/5 + ½ × 2/5 = 1/2.
Then reverse. The probability that the red ball came from bag 1 is P(bag 1) P(red | bag 1) ÷ P(red) = (½ × 3/5) ÷ (1/2) = 3/5.

Count tables avoid formulas. Take 1000 people, 1% have a disease: 10 have it, 990 do not. A test is positive for 90% of those with the disease (9) and for 10% of those without it (99). A person who tests positive has probability 9/(9 + 99) = 1/12 of having the disease.

A tree diagram multiplies along each path and adds the paths that lead to the evidence. The probability of each cause given the evidence is the path value for that cause divided by the sum of the path values that give the evidence.
Do not confuse the two directions: P(positive | disease) = 0.9 is not P(disease | positive) = 1/12.

deepDiveAspects.title: Base rates
deepDiveAspects.content: A rare cause with an accurate test can still have a low posterior, because false positives from the large healthy group swamp the true positives.

deepDiveAspects.title: Sequential updating
deepDiveAspects.content: The posterior after one piece of evidence becomes the prior for the next.

solvedExamples.title: Which bag?
solvedExamples.question: Bag 1 has 3 red and 2 blue balls and bag 2 has 2 red and 3 blue. A bag is chosen at random and a red ball is drawn. Find the probability that it came from bag 1.

solvedExamples.title: Medical test
solvedExamples.question: 1% of people have a disease. A test is positive for 90% of the sick and for 10% of the healthy. What is the probability that a person who tests positive is sick?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: False positives from the large healthy group dominate.

solvedExamples.title: Machine and defect
solvedExamples.question: Machine A makes 60% of items with 2% defective, machine B makes 40% with 5% defective. An item is found defective. What is the probability that it was made by A?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: B has the higher defect rate, so it is more likely.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Take N = 1000 (or a multiple), split by priors, apply likelihoods, and divide the cause count by the evidence total.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the prior as the answer

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Using the likelihood of one cause.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: The posteriors of all causes must sum to 1.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Use a count table with N = 1000 or 10000.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Bayes questions look hard but are two multiplications and a division.

advanced.question: A test for a disease has 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity. If 1% of people have the disease, a person who tests positive is sick with probability
advanced.explanation: Per 10000: 99 true positives and 99 false positives: 99/198 = 1/2.

advanced.question: A student knows the answer to 60% of the questions; otherwise he guesses among 4 choices. He answers a question correctly. The probability that he knew the answer is
advanced.explanation: P(correct) = 0.6 + 0.4 × 0.25 = 0.7. Posterior = 0.6/0.7 = 6/7, so the answer is 6/7.
